summary:
Luna Site Navigator is a web application that allows exploration and comparison of landing sites and coordinates on the Moon. You can pick any point on the 3D, 2D, or orbit view of the Moon, and it will show the conditions there on a chosen date. If no date is picked, then it will default to the current date. Conditions include how high the Sun and Earth sit above the horizon, the length of sunlight over 30 days, ground elevation, terrain, surface temperature, and the distance to the nearest ice region. 
There are three modes, starting with general, which allows the general public to easily control the time/date and compare different sites or coordinates side-by-side with basic information about the locations. The advanced section starts with mission needs called attributes. These attributes can be ticked on or off and will show the best-fitting sites from the 32 past and planned landing sites. Finally, the game section is a GeoGuessr-style challenge that uses real mission photos to locate sites on the Moon. General and Advanced each have an interactive tutorial.
The goal of the entire project is to make lunar site selection understandable to students and the general public, and to provide mission planners with data to make informed decisions by comparing the trade-offs between sunlight availability, Earth visibility, and other landing-site conditions across different locations and mission priorities.
details:
Project Y.U.R.I - LunaSite provides information about the Moon and landing sites at different levels of experience. It serves both the general public and expert users. With this project, we hope to educate the masses about the Moon. It can also help mission planners choose landing sites for future Moon missions. 

Users click on an interactive 3D Moon, or type in coordinates and a date. They are then presented with various data, such as how high the Sun and Earth sit above the horizon, the elevation and terrain, and how conditions change over the next 30 days. The Finder searches the Moon for sites that meet a user’s requirements, such as sunlight, slope, elevation, and line of sight to Earth. Users can also compare sites side by side. A weighted ranking system allows users to decide the weightings of certain parameters. It then scores 32 past and/or planned landing sites using NASA JPL Horizons data. A general mode explains the numbers in plain words, and an advanced mode shows full angles and timelines. 

Sun and Earth angles come from NASA JPL Horizons when the Python (FastAPI) backend is running, and from a built-in model otherwise; elevation is read from NASA’s LOLA LDEM_4 dataset. The frontend is HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with three.js. Every value is labeled as measured, retrieved from JPL, or modeled, so users know what they are seeing.

Our project is creative because it turns hard-to-read lunar data into something anyone can explore. It also includes a game where players can test their knowledge to pinpoint where a NASA mission photo was taken.

We considered accessibility for beginners and experts, the accuracy and sources of our data, and honesty about limits. For example, our terrain model is approximate, and results don’t replace professional mission planning.
dataRefs: LOLA gridded elevation, LDEM_4 (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, data set LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0, v3.0)
